_comment: Machine-readable acceptance contract for every exported model.
Hand-authored to mirror docs/web/ASSET-SPECS.md. Deliberately NOT generated
from the build scripts: a checker derived from the builder only ever proves
the builder agrees with itself.
dims_xyz_m are in THREE.JS axes (X right, Y up, Z forward) after the
Blender +Z-up -> glTF +Y-up conversion, so a Blender footprint of
(X=1.0, Y=1.0 flow, Z=0.30 tall) is written here as [1.0, 0.30, 1.0].
Checking it in three.js axes is what proves export_yup actually fired.
Run: python tools/blender/validate_glb.py --all
dims_xyz_m is the T-POSE bounding box: 1.80 m of arm span across X and
1.80 m of height. ASSET-SPECS 3.1 lists 0.60 x 0.40 x 1.80, which is
the standing FOOTPRINT and is carried by col_Player, not by the mesh.
pivot_tolerance_m 0.03: the feet sit exactly on y = 0 and the mesh is
exactly centred on x, but a character's depth centroid is not its
ground pivot - the chest pack and the boots run forward of it.
rest_pose is the rigged form of the frame-1 identity rule: a walk
cycle's frame 1 is mid-stride and cannot be the identity, so instead
the armature exports at bind and every clip is relative to it.
2026-07-27 (W11 lane A): X = 1.80 arm span and Y = 1.80 height are the
character's REAL size and stay exact; they are bone-driven and a client
capsule and eye height are set against them. Z is the depth envelope and
was raised 0.39 -> 0.46 to buy a back pack and a deeper chest, which is
a silhouette change and not an interface one. pivot_tolerance_m 0.03 ->
0.05 for the same reason: a back pack moves the depth centroid, and the
pivot rule that matters (feet exactly on y = 0, exactly centred on x) is
unchanged.
pivot_mode 'none': the origin is the CAMERA POINT, so the model
attaches to the camera with an identity transform and the mesh hangs
below and in front of an origin that is deliberately outside it.
The bone names and hierarchy are the body rig's arm subset exactly,
which is the contract that lets one animation layer drive both. The
BIND POSE is not shared: this one is the view-model rest.
No collision and no LOD chain: first person is always near.
2026-07-27 (W11 lane A): Reid reported the on-screen hands read as
'large white mitts'. The fix is a framing one, so the declared envelope
moved: the hands sit FURTHER from the camera and lower, the elbows come
in, and the glove stops being the same pale Suit white as the body.
tolerance_m is 0.02 here and 0.005 everywhere else, deliberately. The
envelope check exists to prove export_yup fired and that nothing
overhangs a footprint. A view model has no footprint, no grid, no mating
plane and no placement arithmetic: its envelope is a did-it-explode
bound, not an interface, so pinning it to 5 mm would only buy friction
on an asset that is tuned by looking at it. Every other asset keeps
W11 lane A, 2026-07-27. Four wearable slots: head, chest, legs, feet.
THE NODE NAMES ARE SLOT NAMES, NOT SET NAMES. A second armour set is a
second .glb carrying the same four node names, so the client's slot
lookup is set-independent and swapping a set is swapping a file. That
is the whole reason this file is not called armour_tier1.
SKINNED, NOT BONE-PARENTED. Each slot is a skinned mesh carrying the
SAME 44-bone armature as player_body.glb, the same bone names, the same
order and the same T-pose rest, all read from rig_common.BODY_BONES
rather than retyped. So a leg plate bends at the knee, a chest plate
rides the spine, and the client binds each slot to the skeleton it
already has instead of parenting twenty rigid props to twenty bones.
bones[] and rest_pose below are what make that a checked property and
not a hope: if the two rigs ever drift, this file fails.
pivot_mode 'none': an armour piece hangs at its own bone's height, so
a helmet's base is at y = 1.50 and a ground pivot is meaningless. Same
reasoning as the first-person arms.
tolerance_m 0.02, not 0.005, and for the same reason the view model has
it: armour has no footprint, no grid and no mating plane. Its envelope
is a did-it-explode bound. The fit that actually matters is armour
against the body surface, and that is judged by rendering the two
together, which is what a bounding box cannot do.
LOD0 ONLY, deliberately. web/src/player/Avatar.ts:55-62 loads the body
with lod: '_LOD0' and there is exactly one player, so the body's own
LOD1 and LOD2 are already dead weight. Shipping three bands here would
triple the skinning payload to make the same picture. Revisit when
multiplayer puts more than one character on screen.
NO REFERENT IN THE HEADLESS HEADERS. gameplay.h has no equipment slots,
no armour items and no ItemCategory for them: grepping core/include for
armor|armour|equip returns nothing. Built on Reid's direct request, the
same situation as the structural set in BT-9, and escalated to Admin.
pivot_mode 'grip': the origin is the grip point 0.30 m up the haft,
so hand.add(tool) with an identity transform puts it in the fist.
The check asserts socket_grip lands on the origin AND that the origin
is inside the mesh bounds, which is the pair of facts that make the
identity attach correct rather than merely plausible.
Fourteen sibling meshes, no LOD chain, no collision, no clips.
pivot_mode 'centre': an item's origin is its volumetric centre, not
its base, because items tumble when dropped and ride centred on a
belt. Every mesh sits ON the origin (they overlap) so a consumer can
clone one by name with no offset to subtract back out.
The per-part block is the real gate here: one lod0_node check would
prove nothing about the other thirteen.
2026-07-27 (W11 lane A, belt cargo). Two additions, both because these
meshes stop being icons and start riding belts.
1. Every Item_* node gains a CHILD Empty named socket_rest, at the
item's own lowest point on its vertical axis. Placing an item on a
belt is then 'beltPoint minus socket_rest.position', one subtraction
with no per-item height table anywhere. The socket names all dedupe
to socket_rest, so the runtime rule is the same one rocket_parts.glb
publishes: clone the PART node and query the clone.
2. Item_Crate is new: one generic packed crate that carries any
ItemCategory::Buildable on a belt. The alternative was scaling a
machine mesh down to fit, and a 4 m foundation at 0.24 m is a smudge.
The FLOW-AXIS extent rule lives in tools/blender/check_belt_cargo.py,
because factory_sim.h's kItemSpacing = 64 of kUnitsPerTile = 256 means
saturated items are 0.250 m apart and an item wider than that along the
flow axis interpenetrates its neighbour.
TIER 1. One atlas per biome (ASSET-SPECS 3.2): the scatter system
wants one file per biome and one InstancedMesh per prop.
Every prop is a sibling mesh sitting ON the origin, base at y = 0,
so a scatter placement matrix is pure terrain data with no per-prop
offset. The per-part block with pivot 'ground' is what proves that,
and it is the real gate here - one lod0_node check would say nothing
about the other three.
LOD0 and LOD2 only: props skip the middle band.
Collision is per-prop and DELIBERATELY PARTIAL. Only solid obstacles
carry a proxy; shells and dune grass are walk-through, because a
collider on ankle-height dressing is the player snagging on scenery.
TIER 1, Biome::Plains. Six props across three scale bands.
Only Plains_PebbleB collides. Both grass tufts, the flowers, the
small pebble and the shrub are walk-through: plains scatter is the
densest in the game and a player pushing through grass must not
feel it.
TIER 1, Biome::Forest. Explicitly the FLOOR of the forest and the
DEAD wood in it: the two live trees are harvest nodes, and a scatter
prop that looked like one would read as a node the player cannot
chop.
col_Forest_DeadTree is the TRUNK box only (0.50 x 0.50 x 4.20), the
same rule the conifer follows: a player walks through where the
branches were.
TIER 1, Biome::Hills - the prime ore zone. Hills_LargeBoulder is
2.3 m across, deliberately bigger than the 1.7 m coal boulder that
is the largest harvest node, so scenery and node are never confused.
Only the boulder collides.
TIER 1, Biome::Mountains. Three roles is the smallest palette of any
atlas and it is deliberate: above the tree line there is stone and
snow and nothing else, and the renderer batches by material.
Mtn_RockSpire is the only Tier-1 prop that reads at 200 m.
The snow patch is a surface, not an obstacle: walk-through.
TIER 1, Biome::Polar. The one biome where prop and terrain share a
colour, so silhouette carries everything: the shard is sharply
vertical, the drift strongly directional, and the ice boulder keeps
dark stone showing on its flanks so it is visible at all.
The drift is walk-over.
TIER 1, Biome::Ocean. Two props is correct, not thin: biome.h gives
ocean a spawn probability of zero, so nothing is harvested there and
the seabed is scenery seen through water.
Kelp is walk-through - a player or submersible passes straight
through it.
TIER 1. ONE file covers Biome::Regolith, MoonHighland and
CraterFloor: biome.h classifies the moon by elevation band alone,
the bands abut with no transition, and the surface material is the
same dust everywhere. The scatter pass loads one file and picks a
per-biome subset:
Regolith     RockSmall, RockLarge, RegolithRipple
MoonHighland HighlandOutcrop, RockLarge, RockSmall
CraterFloor  CraterRimRock, ImpactGlass, RockSmall
OF_Oil on Moon_ImpactGlass is a PBR role, not a substance: impact
melt glass is dark and glossy, and OF_Oil is the palette's only dark
low-roughness surface. OF_Glass would be alpha-blended, and
thousands of alpha-blended instances is a sorting problem bought for
nothing.
TIER 1, and the one atlas not bound to a Biome value: it dresses the
1 m^3 voxel tunnels the player digs.
Cave_SupportFrame is 2.40 m against a 1.80 m player and that is its
job - it is the SCALE REFERENCE that turns a corridor of identical
cubes into a space with a readable height.
Cave_OreVeinPanel is a decal for a dug voxel FACE, so its pivot is
its volumetric centre, not the ground. It carries exactly two
material slots in pinned order, OF_RockDark host then OF_Iron vein,
and the renderer OVERRIDES SLOT 1 per ore type. One mesh, four ores.
Crystals are OF_Glass, never OF_EmissiveState: emissive is reserved
for machine state and genuine fire (ASSET-SPECS 1).
TIER 1, the layer UNDER the biome props: stamped by the square metre
where a biome prop is placed by the handful, so its instance count
is one to two orders of magnitude higher than anything else.
NO LOD CHAIN, deliberately: an 18-triangle card is already at the
floor and there is no distance at which a 0.5 m tuft is worth a
second mesh. The renderer culls the whole layer at its own detail
distance, which is one test rather than one LOD switch per instance.
Nothing collides.
18 to 42 tris each, NOT the 60 to 400 the biome props run at.
Built as tapered blade geometry, not alpha-tested crossed quads:
there is no texture pipeline and an untextured crossed quad renders
as a solid rectangle standing in the grass (spec correction, see
ASSET-SPECS 3.2).
THE VESSEL PART CATALOGUE (DW-29), and the TWO-CLASS STACK CONTRACT.
Twenty-three parts in one file, one group node each, so a renderer
clones the PART and gets its meshes, its sockets and its proxy
together.
TWO DIAMETER CLASSES AND NO MORE. Class S is 1.25 m (R 0.625, 16
segments) and class L is 2.50 m (R 1.250, 24 segments), exactly 2x.
A segment count divisible by 4 puts vertices on +-X and +-Y, so the
exported AABB is exactly the class diameter; a 14-gon at R 0.625
measures 1.250 x 1.244 and misses by 6 mm.
Seventeen stack parts are ground-pivoted on their bottom mating
plane, so socket_stack_bottom is always the origin and stacking is
one addition per part, with no per-part offset table anywhere.
StackAdapter is the ONE part whose two ends differ in class: bottom
L, top S. Without it two classes would be two disjoint catalogues.
Six radial parts (radial decoupler, vernier, fin, RCS, leg, solar
panel) have their origin on their MOUNT PLANE with the body
extending +X, which is neither 'ground' nor 'centre': pivot 'none'
and the dimensions are the check.
SolidBooster is carried radially but is NOT a radial part: it is a
stack part with a socket_radial_attach on its own hull, which mates
with RadialDecoupler's socket_radial_out. Same anti-parallel dot
product as a stack mate, so one rule covers both.
The landing leg and the solar panel are authored STOWED, because the
exported static pose is frame 1 of the deploy clip and a vessel
flies stowed. Each splits into a fixed mesh and an animated one,
because one Blender Action drives one object.
part_sockets is the real gate here: twenty parts carry a
socket_stack_top between them, so a flat presence check proves
nothing. It asserts each socket is under ITS part and lands on the
declared point in three.js axes.
LOD0 only, deliberately: a vessel is either near you or it is a
scaled-scene impostor, and there is no middle band for a part.
TIER 2, and the HERO ASSET of the DW-35 material pass. Rebuilt at
24 x 24 m from the 8 x 8 m original on Reid's 'make it big and make
it look good', which he said twice. 24 is 6 structural cells of the
DW-32 4 m module and 9x the ground area of the original.
A placed structure, so section 2.2 applies exactly as to a smelter:
WHOLE-METRE footprint, pivot at the footprint centre, base on y = 0,
nothing overhanging the cell. 24 is even, so it snaps to a cell
corner.
THE DECK IS RAISED 2.00 m and that is the whole reason the thing
reads as launch infrastructure rather than as a big foundation: it
gives the FLAME TRENCH somewhere to go. A pad flush with the ground
has nowhere to send the exhaust and looks like a car park.
socket_vessel is on the DECK TOP, so it is [0, 2.00, 0]. This is the
rollout anchor that replaces the flight lane's admitted stand-in of
planting a rocket 26 m in front of the player. The value MOVED from
[0, 1.60, 0]; nothing consumed the old one yet.
FOUR clamps, not three, on a 1.90 m circle sized for the DW-29a
class L 2.50 m diameter. The clamp stays a SEPARATE ground-pivoted
part on the file origin, per the Tier-1 atlas convention: the
renderer clones it and places four around the circle socket_clamp
marks.
Clamp_Release is authored HOLDING, because frame 1 is the exported
static pose and a pad at rest is a pad holding a rocket.
THIRTEEN proxies. One convex box cannot describe a slab with a 28 m
mast on one edge, and the trench must NOT be filled in by the deck
proxy or the player walks on air over it. Five of them are the
structure: the two deck banks, the launch table that legitimately
spans the trench, the tower and the clamp.
THE OTHER EIGHT ARE THE STAIR TREADS, one each, from the 2026-07-27
playtest: Reid reported that the stairs on the pad do not work.
This list used to omit col_LaunchMount, which the file has always
shipped, and to declare nothing at all for the stairs, which the file
never shipped: the notch in the north-east corner was drawn and had no
collision under it, so the only route onto the deck on foot was a
2.72 m stretch of thin air ending in a 2.00 m wall. The client reads
proxies off the FILE and not off this list, so the omission cost
nothing by itself; what it cost was the check that would have caught
the stairs. web/scripts/check-proxies.mjs now compares this set
against what every .glb actually ships, in both directions.
The tread proxies are AXIS-ALIGNED boxes because that is all
StructureBody.ts can express, and there is one per drawn tread so the
surface you stand on is the surface you can see. 156 collision
triangles against a budget of 160; none of them reach a pixel.
TIER 2, the Cinder outpost beat (ObjectiveStep::OutpostComplete).
A LANDMARK rather than a part, so it carries the full LOD chain that
rocket_parts.glb deliberately does not: this is what a player
navigates back to from 200 m away.
Assembled from the SHIPPED parts through hc.Parts transforms, with
the legs and panels in their deployed pose, so it cannot drift away
from the flyable vessel.
6.40 m tall and 4.08 m across the feet. The stack heights are what
the legs allow: the foot lands 2.13 m below its hinge, so the hinge
sits 2.20 m up and the engine bell clears the ground by 0.30 m.
All three LODs sit on exactly the same ground plane; a LOD switch
that sinks the lander two centimetres is visible from the hatch.
The proxy is the CORE STACK, not the leg span: a convex box over 4 m
of mostly air is a wall the player cannot walk under.
TIER 2, GEOMETRY ONLY: the shader is the rendering domain's.
A UNIT plume, 1.00 m across the mouth and 1.00 m long, pointing down
three.js +Z, which is what a socket's facing is. So it attaches with
socket_muzzle.add(plume) at IDENTITY and is scaled
(exitDiameter, exitDiameter, plumeLength).
The origin is the MOUTH, not the centre and not the base, so throttle
is a scale on Z alone and the mouth stays welded to the bell:
pivot 'none'.
THE ONLY ASSET IN THE GAME WITH UVs. U wraps 0..1 with the seam on
+X; V is 0 at the mouth and 1 at the tip, linear in LENGTH. Authored
flipped, because the exporter writes 1 - v, so that the SHIPPED file
reads the way this comment says it does.
OF_EmissiveState is the palette role for genuine fire. Backface-
culled as authored: DOUBLE_SIDED is palette-wide, and adding
EmissiveState to it would double-side every machine's state chip.
TIER 2, the scaled far-scene body. A UNIT icosphere at three
subdivision levels: 1280 / 320 / 80 triangles.
RADIUS COMES FROM BodyParams, never from the mesh. The renderer
scales by radiusM (Forge 600 km, Cinder 200 km, orbital.h), so one
mesh serves every body and dims are [2, 2, 2] by definition.
Icosphere, not UV sphere: a UV sphere pinches half its vertices into
the poles, which is exactly where a polar orbit flies over.
The mesh is INSCRIBED: every vertex is on radius 1.0, so every face
sags below it by 0.45% at LOD0, 1.78% at LOD1 and 6.58% at LOD2. A
renderer that needs the horizon exact scales by radiusM * (1 + sag).
pivot 'centre': a body is positioned by its centre, not stood on the
ground. One material; the renderer recolours base colour per body.
TIER 0 BASE BUILDING, the deck family. Module 1 x 1 x 0.50 m.
ANCHOR: a CELL CENTRE, floor(x) + 0.5, exactly like a 1x1 machine.
The parts list checks LOD1 and LOD2 on the same box as LOD0, because
a tiling part whose far LOD is a different size shows a seam opening
up as the player walks away, and the single lod0_node check would
never see it.
RESCALED 2026-07-26 (DW-32, decision BT-11): CELL 1.00 -> 4.00 m.
DECK_H stays 0.50 because a deck thickness is set by what a deck IS,
not by the plan module: 4 x 4 x 0.50 is the same 8:1 slab a 1 m deck
was at 2:1, and scaling it would have given a 2 m plinth.
The storey pitch identity DECK_H + WALL_H = STOREY = 4.00 m is
asserted in structure_common.py, and STOREY now EQUALS CELL, so the
plan lattice and the vertical lattice are one 4 m number.
TIER 0 BASE BUILDING. The SAME 4 x 4 x 0.50 m envelope as the
foundation, deliberately: a deck of two thicknesses would give the
storey pitch two values.
THIS PART IS ALSO THE CEILING. There is no ceiling.glb; storey N's
ceiling is storey N+1's floor at z = 4(N+1), same part, same origin.
That is why the ribs are underneath and the plate on top.
TIER 0 BASE BUILDING, the wall family. Module 4.00 wide x 0.25 thick
x 3.50 m tall.
ANCHOR: a CELL EDGE MIDPOINT, not a cell centre. The panel is centred
on its own origin across the thickness (which is what the ground
pivot check asserts), so putting that origin on the edge line makes
one wall serve both cells it divides and makes four walls close
exactly around one foundation.
RESCALED 2026-07-26 (DW-32, BT-11). WALL_T stays 0.25 for the same
reason DECK_H stays 0.50: a wall is as thick as a wall is, and a 1 m
thick partition is a bunker. Only the PLAN module scaled.
dims [4.0, 3.50, 0.25]: the 3.50 landing on three.js Y is what proves
export_yup fired, and it is the number that must equal STOREY - DECK_H.
TIER 0 BASE BUILDING. The wall module with a 1.20 x 2.40 m opening,
so it drops into any cell of any wall run with no special case.
THE DOOR IS STILL ONE FULL CELL, and at a 4 m cell that is the whole
decision (DW-32, BT-11). The MODULE scaled and the OPENING did not:
a 4 m opening is a garage, and a sub-cell door would need a second,
finer lattice for wall furniture that no part of the placement
system has. So the panel is 4 m and the hole in it is 1.20 m, which
is a double-leaf industrial doorway against a 0.60 m player.
THREE collision proxies, not one: a convex hull of a doorway is a
sealed wall. Two jambs and a header leave the opening walk-through.
The 40 mm hazard threshold is a step-over and carries none.
Door_Leaf hangs off door_hinge at x = -0.60 (the left jamb's inner
face) and is the only animated node. frame1_identity asserts the
exported static pose is a CLOSED door.
OF_Accent appears here and NOWHERE else in the structural set: the
orange lintel band is what makes the way in findable across a base.
TIER 0 BASE BUILDING, DW-32's support pillar. Four ground-pivoted
parts on the file origin, one group node each, assembled by the
renderer: a pillar is not one asset, it is a RECIPE.
WHY NOT ONE STRETCHED MESH. A pillar spans whatever gap there is
between an overhanging foundation's underside and the ground, which
is a continuous number, and one mesh scaled to it stretches its foot
and its bracket along with its shaft.
THE SHAFT IS PRISMATIC, which is the whole trick: constant cross
section along Y, no vertical feature anywhere on it, so scaling it in
Y is not an approximation, it is exact. Nothing can distort because
there is nothing along the axis to distort. Authored at EXACTLY
1.00 m so scale.y IS the length in metres.
The rhythm comes from PillarCollar, repeated every 2.00 m and never
scaled, which is what stops a long pillar reading as a stretched
tube. Foot and head are fixed heights at the two ends.
ASSEMBLY, given gap H from ground to deck underside:
H < 0.70          no pillar at all, the deck is close enough
PillarFoot        y = 0,        0.40 tall
PillarShaft       y = 0.40,     scale.y = H - 0.70
PillarHead        y = H - 0.30, 0.30 tall
PillarCollar      y = 0.40 + 2.00k, k = 1.., dropped if within
0.35 m of either end
LOD0 ONLY, and it is a floor rather than an omission: the shaft is
16 triangles and the collar 24, which is already below where a
decimator saves anything. Same call detail_cards.glb makes.
